Ben reviews each lesson before it is marked done. ::: ::: {.cell context='setup'} ```{webr} #| results: markup #| warning: false #| message: false #| include: true #| context: setup #| label: unnamed-chunk-2 options(mc.cores = 1) ``` ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false import {dnorm, rng, palette} from "./widgets/irt.js" import {catNodes, makeBank, info2pl, runCat, mle2pl, simulateCats, normalThetas} from "./widgets/item-banks-cat.js" import {quiz, predict} from "./widgets/quiz.js" ``` ## What this is for A collection of calibrated items is an **item bank**, and its most demanding use is **computerized adaptive testing** (CAT): each item is chosen after the last answer, to suit the respondent. [Information, precision, and short forms](information.qmd) picked the most informative items for one point on the scale; a CAT does that again after every response, at the respondent's current estimate. This lesson builds the loop from information and the EAP, asks what stopping rules buy and what choosing by information costs, and runs adaptive tests after the fact on a medical examination and the PROMIS depression items. A CAT is only as good as the bank is where the respondent sits. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [What is measurement?](measurement.qmd): one of the things we want from a measure is that it give precise information quickly, with few items. Adaptive testing is the most direct attempt at "quickly". ::: ## Goals By the end of this lesson you should be able to: - say what an item bank holds and what keeping one up involves; - run the adaptive loop: start, choose by information, score by EAP, stop; - compare fixed-length, standard-error and classification stopping rules; - explain what maximum information does to item exposure, and what the fixes cost; - run a post-hoc CAT on real responses and read it as a statement about the bank. ## Core ideas ### An item bank What does a bank store? At the least, each item and its calibrated parameters, fixed, so that a respondent's $\theta$ can be estimated from any subset of the items and lands on the bank's scale ([Wainer et al., 2000](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781410605931); [van der Linden & Glas, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-85461-8)). A working bank also records each item's content codes, dates, how often it has been given, and the checks it has passed. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [The Rasch model](rasch.qmd): outfit and infit are near 1 if the model is right; well below 1 an item *overfits* (it is more predictable than the model expects), well above 1 it *underfits*. A bank screens its items with statistics like these. ::: If you've done [Model fit and out-of-sample prediction](fit-prediction.qmd), outfit's spread under a true model shrinks with sample size, so the screening rule should depend on the calibration sample. If you've done [Differential item functioning](dif.qmd), each item also gets a DIF screen, which needs group memberships in the calibration data. If you've done [Linking and equating](equating.qmd), new items join the bank's scale by calibration alongside old ones acting as anchors. A bank is maintained, not finished: overused items are retired, old items checked for drift, new ones added. ### The adaptive loop ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [Information, precision, and short forms](information.qmd): a 2PL item's information is $a^2P(1-P)$, largest at $\theta = b$; test information adds across items, and the conditional SEM is $1/\sqrt{I(\theta)}$. ::: How do we choose items for someone whose $\theta$ we don't yet know? One at a time ([Lord, 1980, ch. 10](https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615); [Weiss, 1982](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662168200600408)): 1. **Start** at the population mean. 2. **Choose** the unused item most informative at the current estimate, and give it. 3. **Update** the estimate from every response so far. 4. **Stop** when a rule says so; otherwise go back to 2. Step 3 has a problem at the start. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [Estimating abilities](ability-estimation.qmd): an all-right or all-wrong pattern has no maximum-likelihood estimate; the EAP, the posterior mean under a normal prior, exists for every pattern. ::: After one item every pattern is all-right or all-wrong, so there is no MLE until the respondent has one of each; the EAP exists throughout, and adaptive testing and Bayesian scoring grew up together ([Owen, 1975](https://doi.org/10.2307/2285821); [Bock & Mislevy, 1982](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662168200600405)). Adapting is older than computers: [Binet and Simon (1904)](https://doi.org/10.3406/psy.1904.3675) graded their tasks by the age at which children pass them, and individually given tests still start at a basal level and stop at a ceiling. #### Try it: one CAT, step by step A 100-item 2PL bank and one simulated respondent. Write $p_k(\theta)$ for the posterior after $k$ items, with mean $\hat\theta_k$ and variance $\sigma_k^2$. **What we would like to minimize.** If a CAT stops on the posterior SD, a natural choice of next item $j$ is the one that leaves the smallest posterior variance after its response, averaged over the responses it might get: $$\text{EPV}_j = \sum_{x} \Pr(x_j = x \mid \text{responses so far})\; \text{Var}(\theta \mid \text{responses so far},\, x_j = x),$$ where $\Pr(x_j = x \mid \cdot) = \int \Pr(x_j = x \mid \theta)\,p_k(\theta)\,d\theta$. [Owen (1975)](https://doi.org/10.2307/2285821) selected items with a normal approximation to the posterior; [van der Linden (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294775) sets out selection criteria that use the posterior itself. **Why maximum information approximates it.** Suppose the posterior is close to normal and narrow enough that item $j$'s information barely changes across it. Then one more response adds about $I_j(\hat\theta_k)$ to the posterior's precision, as a normal likelihood carrying that information would: $$\frac{1}{\sigma_{k+1}^2} \approx \frac{1}{\sigma_k^2} + I_j(\hat\theta_k).$$ The right-hand side increases with $I_j(\hat\theta_k)$, so the item with the most information at the EAP is, approximately, the item that shrinks the posterior most. **When they part.** Early in the test the posterior is wide ($\sigma_0 = 1$), and a steep item's information is concentrated in a band much narrower than that: an item with $a = 2.4$ has lost about 70% of its peak information one logit from its $b$. What matters then is information averaged over where $\theta$ might be, $\int I_j(\theta)\,p_k(\theta)\,d\theta$, which can favour a flatter item near the posterior's centre. [Chang and Ying (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662169602000303) argue that information at the estimate is least suited to the start of a test, and propose a global (Kullback–Leibler) information for the early items. As responses accumulate, the posterior narrows, the approximation improves, and the criteria agree. ::: ### Stopping rules When should a CAT stop? Three answers are standard ([Weiss & Kingsbury, 1984](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1984.tb01040.x)). - **Fixed length.** Everyone gets, say, 20 items: predictable time, easy content balance, precision that varies along the scale. - **Target standard error.** Stop when the posterior SD reaches, say, 0.3, with a cap on length: equal precision wherever the bank can deliver it, and varying length. - **Classification.** For a pass/fail decision, stop once the responses favour one side of the cut clearly enough (callout below). If you've done [What does a score mean?](score-meaning.qmd), this spends the items near the cut, where classification is uncertain. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Go deeper: stopping for a pass/fail decision **Assumptions:** known item parameters; local independence; one cut $\theta_c$ and an indifference region $\theta_c \pm \delta$ within which either decision is acceptable; tolerated error rates $\alpha$ (failing someone at $\theta_c + \delta$) and $\beta$ (passing someone at $\theta_c - \delta$). **The test.** After $k$ items, compare the likelihood of the responses at the two edges of the region, $$\Lambda_k = \frac{L(\theta_c + \delta \mid x_1, \dots, x_k)}{L(\theta_c - \delta \mid x_1, \dots, x_k)}.$$ [Wald's (1945)](https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177731118) sequential probability ratio test stops and passes the respondent once $\Lambda_k \ge (1 - \beta)/\alpha$, stops and fails them once $\Lambda_k \le \beta/(1 - \alpha)$, and otherwise gives another item. With $\alpha = \beta = 0.05$ the bounds are 19 and 1/19. **Which items.** Every item moves $\log\Lambda$ by $\log[P_i(\theta_c+\delta)/P_i(\theta_c-\delta)]$ if right and by the corresponding ratio of $1 - P_i$ if wrong, so the items that move it most sit near the cut, whatever the current estimate. Choosing by information at the cut is the simple rule; [Eggen (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1177/01466219922031365) compares it with Kullback–Leibler information, and [Spray and Reckase (1996)](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986021004405) compare the SPRT with a Bayesian sequential rule. Respondents far from the cut are classified in a few items; those near it take the longest, and a cap decides what happens to them. Problem 5 tries it on the CMSCE. ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [Estimating abilities](ability-estimation.qmd): the EAP is pulled toward the prior mean, most where the likelihood is flattest, and its standard error is the posterior SD. ::: A standard-error rule stops on the posterior SD, and the posterior includes the prior: where the bank is thin, part of the precision it counts is the prior's, and the estimate that stops has been pulled toward the mean. (Between fixed forms and a CAT sit **multistage tests**, which adapt between short preassembled modules; [Luecht & Nungester, 1998](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1998.tb00537.x).) #### Try it: stopping rules and the shape of the bank A 150-item bank whose difficulties you place; 25 simulated respondents at each true $\theta$ from −3 to 3 (target-SE tests stop at 60 items at most). ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof c2_mean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Bank: mean difficulty"}) viewof c2_sd = Inputs.range([0.3, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Bank: SD of difficulties"}) viewof c2_rule = Inputs.radio(["Fixed length", "Target standard error"], {value: "Fixed length", label: "Stopping rule"}) viewof c2_len = Inputs.range([5, 60], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Length (fixed rule)"}) viewof c2_se = Inputs.range([0.2, 0.5], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "Target SE"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false c2_thetas = [-3, -2.5, -2, -1.5, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3] c2_bank = makeBank(150, c2_mean, c2_sd, 11) c2_rows = simulateCats(c2_bank, c2_thetas, 25, c2_rule === "Fixed length" ? Everyone sees the same first item and respondents who answer alike see the same next ones, so a few steep items go to almost everyone; where a test has stakes, such items become known. And information knows nothing about content: a CAT on a medical examination could spend every item on one specialty unless told otherwise. The fixes trade precision for control ([Revuelta & Ponsoda, 1998](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1998.tb00541.x), compare eight). **Randomesque** selection picks at random among the few most informative items ([Kingsbury & Zara, 1989](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15324818ame0204_6)). **Sympson–Hetter** gives each selected item a probability of being administered, tuned by simulation to cap its exposure ([Hetter & Sympson, 1997](https://doi.org/10.1037/10244-014); [van der Linden, 2003](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986028003249)). **a-stratification** splits the bank by slope and moves from the flattest stratum to the steepest, matching $b$ to the estimate within each ([Chang & Ying, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1177/01466219922031338); [Chang, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-014-9401-5)). #### Try it: who sees which items Five hundred simulated respondents take a 20-item CAT from a 100-item bank. Each dot is an item, at its difficulty and the share of respondents who saw it. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof c3_rule = Inputs.radio(["Randomesque", "a-stratified"], {value: "Randomesque", label: "Compare maximum information with"}) viewof c3_top = Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Randomesque: choose among the top"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false c3_bank = makeBank(100, 0, 1, 11) c3_th = normalThetas(500, 3) c3_expo = rows => { const c = new Array(100).fill(0); rows.forEach(d => d.ids.forEach(i => c[i]++)); return c.map(v => v / rows.length); } c3_rmse = rows => Math.sqrt(rows.reduce((s, d) => s + (d.eap - d.theta) ** 2, 0) / rows.length) c3_max = simulateCats(c3_bank, c3_th, 1, {maxItems: 20}, 9) c3_alt = simulateCats(c3_bank, c3_th, 1, c3_rule === "Randomesque" ? {maxItems: 20, top: c3_top} : {maxItems: 20, select: "astrat"}, 9) c3_label = c3_rule === "Randomesque" ? `Randomesque, top ${c3_top}` : "a-stratified" c3_e1 = c3_expo(c3_max) c3_e2 = c3_expo(c3_alt) Plot.plot({ width: 700, height: 280, x: {label: "Item difficulty b", domain: [-3, 3]}, y: {label: "Share of respondents who saw it", domain: [0, 1]}, color: {legend: true, domain: ["Maximum information", c3_label], range: [palette.light, palette.contrast]}, marks: [ Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}), Plot.dot(c3_bank, {x: "b", y: it => c3_e1[it.id], r: it => 2 + 1.5 * it.a, fill: () => "Maximum information", fillOpacity: 0.8}), Plot.dot(c3_bank, {x: "b", y: it => c3_e2[it.id], r: it => 2 + 1.5 * it.a, stroke: () => c3_label, fill: "none", strokeWidth: 1.5}) ] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false c3_sum = (e, rows) => `most-seen item ${(100 * Math.max(...e)).toFixed(0)}%, ${e.filter(v => v > 0.5).length} items seen by more than half, ${e.filter(v => v === 0).length} never used, RMSE ${c3_rmse(rows).toFixed(2)}` md`**Maximum information:** ${c3_sum(c3_e1, c3_max)}. **${c3_label}:** ${c3_sum(c3_e2, c3_alt)}. Larger dots are steeper items.` ``` Under maximum information one item goes to everyone, 17 go to more than half, and 38 of the 100 are never used; the most exposed are steep items near the middle. Randomesque selection among the top five brings the most-seen item down only to 87%, with 30 unused and no loss of precision. a-stratification spreads the load much further (3 items seen by more than half, 9 unused) at a cost: the RMSE rises from 0.28 to 0.34, because the steep items wait. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz({ q: "Why does a-stratification cost precision in the widget, while randomesque selection among the top five doesn't?", options: [ {text: "a-stratification gives flat items early, when steep ones would tell more", correct: true, why: "Information goes with $a^2$. The difference is which 20."} ] }) ``` ### Everything rests on the bank's parameters A CAT puts every respondent's different test on one scale, which works only if the bank's parameters, estimated from particular respondents taking a particular form, hold for other respondents and other combinations of items. If you've done [Parameter invariance](parameter-invariance.qmd), that lesson tested this property. The ROAR-CAT project checked it before going live ([Ma et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-024-02578-y)): it calibrated a reading bank in four groups of students, removed six items that functioned differently across them, and then randomly assigned students to random or CAT order. To reach a reliability of 0.9, 75 CAT items did the work of 125 random ones. A cheaper check uses data already in hand: a **post-hoc CAT**. Calibrate on some respondents who answered every item, and let a CAT choose items for the others, revealing only the responses it asks for; then compare its estimate with the whole bank's, respondent by respondent. The unchosen items are missing by design, which is ignorable given the model ([Mislevy & Wu, 1996](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.1996.tb01708.x)). What it can't show is whether respondents answer an item the same way inside a CAT as inside the fixed form. ## Simulate The code below gives 200 simulated respondents a CAT from a 200-item 2PL bank (EAP, maximum information, stop at a posterior SD of 0.3 or 60 items), and compares it with a fixed form of the 20 items most informative at $\theta = 0$. It is base R and runs in a second or two. With the seed as written, the CAT uses 13.65 items on average against the form's 20, with RMSEs of 0.29 and 0.31. The averages hide a trade: in the middle ($-0.5$ to $0.5$) the fixed form is more precise (0.22 against 0.29), since the CAT stops at 0.3 after about 10 items; above 1.5 the CAT is (0.30 against 0.47), using 26 items. The form spends its items where most respondents are; the CAT spends them where each respondent is. Try `se_stop <- 0.2`, or `b <- rnorm(n_items, 1.5, 0.5)`, a bank built for a high cut. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} #| results: markup #| warning: false #| message: false #| include: true #| label: unnamed-chunk-17 # Item banks and adaptive testing: simulate a 2PL bank, give each simulated respondent # a CAT (EAP scoring, maximum information, stop when the posterior SD reaches 0.3), and # compare it with one fixed 20-item form from the same bank. Base R; runs in seconds. set.seed(252) n_items <- 200 # items in the bank n_people <- 200 # respondents se_stop <- 0.3 # stop when the posterior SD reaches this... max_len <- 60 # ...or after this many items form_len <- 20 # length of the fixed form # The bank: difficulties N(0, 1), slopes lognormal around 1.2. Known, as if calibrated. b <- rnorm(n_items, 0, 1) a <- exp(rnorm(n_items, log(1.2), 0.3)) theta <- rnorm(n_people) # Every respondent's answer to every item, generated once: a CAT only reveals some. P <- plogis(outer(theta, b, "-") * matrix(a, n_people, n_items, byrow = TRUE)) X <- (matrix(runif(n_people * n_items), n_people) < P) * 1 nodes <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 101) prior <- dnorm(nodes) eap <- function(ll) { w <- exp(ll - max(ll)) * prior; w <- w / sum(w) th <- sum(nodes * w) c(theta = th, se = sqrt(sum((nodes - th)^2 * w))) } loglik_item <- function(j, x) { # log P(x | node) for item j p <- plogis(a[j] * (nodes - b[j])) if (x == 1) log(p) else log(1 - p) } info <- function(th, j) { p <- plogis(a[j] * (th - b[j])); a[j]^2 * p * (1 - p) } cat_one <- function(x) { ll <- numeric(length(nodes)); used <- integer(0); est <- eap(ll) while (length(used) < max_len && est[["se"]] > se_stop) { avail <- setdiff(seq_len(n_items), used) j <- avail[which.max(info(est[["theta"]], avail))] # most informative at the EAP ll <- ll + loglik_item(j, x[j]) used <- c(used, j); est <- eap(ll) } c(est, n = length(used)) } cat_res <- t(apply(X, 1, cat_one)) # The fixed form: the 20 items most informative at theta = 0, scored by EAP. form <- order(info(0, seq_len(n_items)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:form_len] fixed_res <- t(apply(X, 1, function(x) eap(Reduce(`+`, lapply(form, function(j) loglik_item(j, x[j])))))) rmse <- function(est, keep = TRUE) sqrt(mean((est[keep] - theta[keep])^2)) band <- cut(theta, c(-Inf, -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, Inf)) round(data.frame( respondents = as.vector(table(band)), cat_items = tapply(cat_res[, "n"], band, mean), cat_rmse = sapply(levels(band), function(l) rmse(cat_res[, "theta"], band == l)), fixed20_rmse = sapply(levels(band), function(l) rmse(fixed_res[, "theta"], band == l)), row.names = levels(band)), 2) c(cat_mean_items = mean(cat_res[, "n"]), cat_rmse = round(rmse(cat_res[, "theta"]), 3), fixed20_rmse = round(rmse(fixed_res[, "theta"]), 3)) plot(theta, cat_res[, "n"], pch = 16, col = "#2780e3", xlab = "True theta", ylab = "Items given", main = "Items the CAT needed to reach a posterior SD of 0.3") abline(h = form_len, lty = 2, col = "#999999") ``` ::: [Download this code](code/item-banks-cat-sim.R) to run it in your own R session. ## With real data ### A medical examination as a bank Our main example is [choi_2026_cmsce_2020_1](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/choi_2026_cmsce_2020_1/): a 2020 sitting of Korea's Clinical Medical Science Comprehensive Examination (CMSCE) for medical students ([Choi et al., 2026, data](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/TQZQ6L)). Its job is to be a real bank for a post-hoc CAT. The items are five-option multiple choice across seven clinical domains, scored 1 for correct, and [Choi et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.29) built a self-assessment CAT from six such sittings. [Download the code](code/item-banks-cat-irw.R); it needs `mirt` ([Chalmers, 2012](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i06)), and the CAT engine is a few dozen lines of base R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(mirt) # Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables//) with a # CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data. cm_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_4:v8_0.choi_2026_cmsce_2020_1/rows?format=csv" df <- read.csv(cm_url) # resp is 1 for a correct answer and 0 otherwise. One sitting per respondent: no waves. cm <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1]) c(respondents = nrow(cm), items = ncol(cm), missing = sum(is.na(cm)), mean_correct = round(mean(cm), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` respondents items missing mean_correct 5388.00 304.00 0.00 0.68 ``` ::: ::: Every student answered every item. We calibrate a 2PL on a random half and keep the other half to be tested. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # Calibrate on a random half; the other half is kept back to take the adaptive test. # mirt writes the 2PL as a*theta + d; our difficulty is b = -d/a (IRTpars = TRUE). set.seed(2020) cal <- sort(sample(nrow(cm), nrow(cm) %/% 2)) m_cm <- mirt(as.data.frame(cm[cal, ]), 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE) pars <- coef(m_cm, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, c("a", "b")] # Items with slopes below 0.3 say little about theta anywhere (information a^2/4 at # most 0.02); they stay out of the bank. bank_items <- rownames(pars)[pars[, "a"] >= 0.3] c(calibration = length(cal), items = nrow(pars), low_slope = sum(pars[, "a"] < 0.3), of_which_negative = sum(pars[, "a"] < 0), bank = length(bank_items)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` calibration items low_slope of_which_negative 2694 304 33 11 bank 271 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} round(quantile(pars[bank_items, "b"], c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 1)), 2) # bank difficulties ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0% 10% 50% 90% 100% -7.15 -2.73 -1.25 0.20 4.21 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} round(quantile(pars[bank_items, "a"], c(0, 0.5, 1)), 2) # bank slopes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0% 50% 100% 0.30 1.05 2.59 ``` ::: ::: Thirty-three items with slopes below 0.3 stay out, leaving 271. Eleven of the 33 have negative slopes, which in a working bank would send them to content review; the scored responses alone can't say why. The bank's median difficulty is −1.25, and only a tenth of its items are harder than 0.20: most are easy for these students. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # A CAT in base R, for any unidimensional model mirt fits. Every quantity lives on a # grid of nodes: the prior, each item's response probabilities and its information. nodes <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 121) prior <- dnorm(nodes) # mirt's calibration fixes the mean at 0 and the SD at 1 make_bank <- function(model, items) { it <- lapply(items, function(i) extract.item(model, i)) list(items = items, logp = lapply(it, function(e) log(probtrace(e, nodes))), # nodes x categories info = sapply(it, function(e) iteminfo(e, nodes))) # nodes x items } # EAP and posterior SD from the log likelihood on the nodes eap <- function(ll) { w <- exp(ll - max(ll)) * prior w <- w / sum(w) th <- sum(nodes * w) c(theta = th, se = sqrt(sum((nodes - th)^2 * w))) } # Each available item's information at theta, interpolated between nodes info_at <- function(bank, th, avail) { k <- findInterval(th, nodes, all.inside = TRUE) f <- (th - nodes[k]) / (nodes[k + 1] - nodes[k]) (1 - f) * bank$info[k, avail] + f * bank$info[k + 1, avail] } # One respondent. x holds their responses (0, 1, ...) to the bank items, in bank order. # Start at the prior mean; give the most informative item at the current EAP (or pick # at random among the `top` most informative, or at random from the whole bank); update; # stop at max_items or when the posterior SD reaches se_stop. run_cat <- function(x, bank, max_items = 20, se_stop = 0, select = "info", top = 1) { ll <- numeric(length(nodes)) used <- integer(0) est <- eap(ll) while (length(used) < max_items && est[["se"]] > se_stop) { avail <- setdiff(seq_along(bank$items), used) if (select == "random") { j <- avail[sample.int(length(avail), 1)] } else { best <- avail[order(info_at(bank, est[["theta"]], avail), decreasing = TRUE)] best <- best[seq_len(min(top, length(best)))] j <- best[sample.int(length(best), 1)] } ll <- ll + bank$logp[[j]][, x[j] + 1] used <- c(used, j) est <- eap(ll) } list(theta = est[["theta"]], se = est[["se"]], n = length(used), used = used) } bank_cm <- make_bank(m_cm, bank_items) ``` ::: The next chunk draws 600 held-out students and computes each one's full-bank EAP, the answer a CAT tries to reach with fewer items. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # The respondents who take the CAT: 600 drawn from the held-out half (the precomputed # run uses all 600; the page runs the first 50 live). held <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(cm)), cal) set.seed(2021) cat_ids <- sample(held, 600) X_cm <- cm[cat_ids, bank_items] # Everyone's full-bank EAP: the target a CAT is trying to reach with fewer items full_cm <- t(apply(X_cm, 1, function(x) unlist(run_cat(x, bank_cm, max_items = length(bank_items))[1:3]))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # Where is the bank informative? When scores go to individuals who act on them, I stop on a target standard error with a cap on length, and I set both from a post-hoc CAT on real responses, as here: it shows where the bank runs out before any respondent does. For this bank, new hard items would buy more than a higher cap. ### PROMIS depression: a bank built for symptoms For contrast, [promis1wave1_depression](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/promis1wave1_depression/): the 56 candidate depression items from the first wave of PROMIS testing, given to US adults ([Cella et al., 2010](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2010.04.011); data at ). The items ask how often, in the past seven days, the respondent had a depressive feeling or thought, from never to always; PROMIS kept 28 in its bank ([Pilkonis et al., 2011](https://doi.org/10.1177/1073191111411667)). None of this is a fault in the respondents or the items: a depression bank is built to tell mild from moderate from severe, which it does in three or four items, and telling "none" from "very few" isn't its job. The examination is thin at the top, the depression bank at the bottom, and in both a post-hoc CAT finds the thin end. ## Problems 1. **Which item next?** (a) Under the Rasch model, show that the most informative item at $\hat\theta$ has $b$ closest to $\hat\theta$.
